hook_text: Up to hundreds of millions of sperm cells set off on the journey. Only one gets to fertilise the egg.
clip_script: Puberty is when hormones switch on the body's reproductive system, at different ages for different people, and that is normal. In males, the testes make millions of sperm every day: tiny cells with a head, a middle and a lashing tail. In females, the ovaries usually release one egg a month: a big cell with its own food store that cannot swim at all. Each month the uterus builds a soft, blood-rich lining. If no egg is fertilised, the lining is shed: a period. But if sperm make the long journey up to the oviduct, only a few hundred reach the egg, and the moment one gets in, the egg seals itself shut. That is fertilisation. The new cell divides, settles into the uterus lining, and a placenta forms to feed the baby for about nine months.
visual_style: Clean whiteboard diagrams of sperm and egg drawn to scale; a simple calendar wheel with the lining building and shedding; a counter dropping from millions to hundreds to one.
pacing: Calm, clear steps with a dramatic countdown at the journey.
